$comment: One row per requirement in PRD.md, naming the evidence that proves it. Generated by hand, enforced by `npm run check:fr-evidence` (scripts/check-fr-evidence.mjs), which fails if an id or title drifts from PRD.md, if a citation points at a file that does not exist, if a browser anchor is not defined by scripts/browser-matrix.mjs, or if a row claims more than it can show. PRD.md is the target and never records status; this file is the status and never restates the target — so no row here repeats requirement text, only cites it.

statesMeaning.met: every clause of the requirement is implemented, tested, documented and guarded
statesMeaning.partial: built, but at least one named clause is not — see gaps
statesMeaning.absent: the clause exists in PRD.md and nothing in the package satisfies it

FR-01.title: Input Flexibility
FR-01.note: Every clause of the row is answered and each refusal has an assertion: the six reasons are `empty`, `bare-name`, `windows-path`, `bad-base64`, `unsupported-scheme` and `no-base-url`. Two decisions worth keeping. The scheme rule is a list of **refusals**, not an allowlist of schemes — an allowlist would refuse `my-app://documents/a.pdf`, which a host’s own desktop shell registers, and would need a release for every new document scheme. And a relative address is refused only where there is no base: the same string classifies as `url` once a page exists, which is asserted as a pair rather than described. `describeSource` lost its "the same origin" subject with that rule, because a refused relative address is the one case where naming an origin would be a lie; a refused scheme names its scheme and echoes nothing after the colon, so a `javascript:` payload stays out of the log line.

FR-02.title: Worker Configuration
FR-02.note: The conflict clause is now enforced: a second viewer asking for a different worker URL is refused before its load starts, with a CONFIGURATION_ERROR that names both origins and nothing else, because a signed worker URL carries its credential in its query. "When it is absent" turns out to be two states, measured on 6.3 and now asserted separately: pdf.js ships './pdf.worker.mjs' in Node and '' in a browser (it assigns from its own isNodeJS), so in Node `ensureWorker` neither probes nor writes and the engine's default *is* the main-thread fallback, while in a browser the field starts empty and the candidate probe is what fills it — which is why README's no-configuration claim is about Vite/webpack/Rollup and not about Node. `worker.default.test.tsx` pins the Node row against the un-mocked engine; writing a probed URL over that default is the cost `worker.fallback.deadurl.test.ts` measures, so the short-circuit is the requirement's own "leave pdf.js's own fallback reachable".

FR-03.title: Password Protection
FR-03.acceptanceWaiver: The encrypted load, the parked promise and the observable re-prompt are proven against the real engine in Node on playground/fixtures/encrypted-sample.pdf; the browser harness has no password check, and the prompt's rendering is covered by the a11y audit instead.

FR-04.title: Cancellation Safety
FR-04.note: The immediate cancel on unmount and scroll-out, the cancellation identified by type that never reaches an ordinary error handler, and the published code set were already asserted. The clause’s last line was not: `extractAllText` threw its own generic `AbortError` for a signal that had already fired, so a host that aborted with “reader navigated away” was handed the platform’s sentence instead of its own and lost the cause. It now goes through the helper the rest of the package uses, keeping `name = AbortError` — every cancellation filter here and in hosts reads that name — and `code = SEARCH_CANCELLED`, and three tests hold the three shapes apart: an `Error` reason, a bare string reason, and no reason at all, which keeps the operation’s own sentence. One site was looked at and deliberately left alone: the walk inside `usePdfSearch` throws the same cancellation into its own catch and answers the host with `idle` and no error, which is this clause’s other sentence and already tested. A reason no consumer can observe is not a promise, so nothing was changed there to make two call sites look symmetrical.

FR-05.title: Viewport Virtualization
FR-05.note: Both clauses have assertions now. Only the visible pages plus an overscan buffer has held since the virtualizer was written — the arithmetic in layout.test.ts, the window in the hook, and the 1,000-page browser row that counts the mounted slots. The placeholder clause is what had no assertion at all: reportPageDims was a vi.fn() in every test that mounted the shell, and the pages that reached the DOM in the suite were hand-built slot lists, so the sentence rested on arithmetic over sizes handed to it. usePdfVirtualizer.dims.test.tsx (7) drives the hook against a viewport with a size in it and asks what a reader would notice: a report sizes its own row and leaves the fit basis alone; a page-1 report moves the fit basis and the scale resolved against it; the first measurement of a page wins, so a stale or repeated report cannot move the layout twice; the rows the sweep has not reached are sized from a sample mean, so the laid-out height at that moment is within 5 % of the one it ends at — and the assertion says what page-1-only sizing would have cost, because that was the 0.8 defect (15 % short on a fixture whose boxes cycle through three shapes, 36 % long before the estimate was a default); and a row growing above the fold moves the scroll position by exactly the growth, so the page at the top of the viewport is still the page that was there. PdfPage.status.test.tsx adds the other end of the same wire: a page reports its scale-1 box, keyed 0-based, once — mounted at 2× and asserted not to report 400×520 — and reports nothing for a proxy that never arrives. Six mutations, each restored byte-for-byte: page-1 sizing for the mean, no scroll compensation, a report that overwrites the last, a fit basis that ignores page 1, a page reporting the box it painted, and a 1-based index. The first four each failed one case in this file; the last two each failed the page cases. Two of them needed a second attempt: the fit-basis mutation was a no-op until the case that reports page 1 existed, and the page mutation did not bite while the component was mounted at scale 1, because at that scale the painted box and the intrinsic box are the same number. #265 moved that clause from jitter to the wrong row. The anchor that keeps a reader in place while a row above them grows derived the reader’s row by looking the element’s `scrollTop` up in the *previous* table, which is right until the document shrinks past them: the engine clamps the position, and the clamped number belongs to the new table. Measured in webkit on `long-sample.pdf` — a jump to page 1000 wrote 1,585,472, because the fit scale was still 1.98, resolved from the 612-wide default box while page 1’s landscape box was in flight; the corrected table shrank the document 27 %; the reader clamped to 1,162,224; and the anchor named the row that number falls on in the stale table, row 733, and moved them there. The matrix row’s own log had been calling that a walk, and the page-change counter #265 added falsified it in one run: two events in ninety seconds, not seven hundred. A jump is now a request that outlives its write — re-issued into each corrected table, bounded by six layout changes, four seconds, or a wheel — and the six cases in `usePdfVirtualizer.jump.test.tsx` hold the whole promise: grow under the reader, shrink past them, keep an in-page destination, yield to a hand scroll, and expire two different ways. Setting the ceiling to one turns five of the six red, each naming the page the the reader lost, and all four browser cells went from a 90 s red to 0.1–0.2 s green.

FR-06.title: Responsive Zoom Modes
FR-06.note: Built and guarded for all four overlay layers. 25 %-500 % and the three fit modes are guarded in src/lib/zoom.ts and layout.test.ts; the text and structure layers were already asserted to take one build and N updates; and src/components/PdfPage.overlay.test.tsx now does the same for the annotation and editor layers, which the page used to destroy and re-create on every scale step. The guard counts constructions, renders and updates, holds the identity of the element the first build stamped, keeps the focus inside the widget across the step, and fires a `change` through the listener the page attaches beside the layer — so “in place” is now four clauses and not a reading of the code. Four counterfactuals, each restoring the source by checksum: the build effect keyed on `viewport` again gives “the zoom rebuilt the annotation layer: expected 3 to have a length of 1” and “the zoom step moved the reader out of the field”; the `update()` call removed gives an empty update list in four tests; the teardown’s `destroy()` removed fails the rotation case; the editor layer left out of the step fails its own count. Measured in chromium on annotated-sample.pdf, eight zoom steps through the toolbar field, with the same probe run against HEAD’s source and this one: 48 elements added and 48 removed per sequence becomes 0 and 0, and 683 ms becomes 637 ms — the wall figure is one sample on this machine, the element count is not. Costs 0.06 kB gz on the shell (64.81 → 64.87) and 0.05 kB on core; `headless` unchanged. In a real engine the same clause is read by the matrix check `zoom-updates-the-layers-in-place`: a MutationObserver on the two layers, four steps through the toolbar field, and the verdict is element churn — HEAD reports 24 replaced and 24 added, this build reports 18 elements in place throughout with 0 and 0, on chromium and firefox desktop and mobile. WebKit is not installed on this host, so its row stays the CI browser job to prove. Two things the same work fixed because the guard noticed them: the annotation layer was never `destroy()`ed when its page rotated or left (only its container was emptied, so the instance and its editable-annotation table outlived it), and the editor layer now rebuilds with it on a programmatic form write, because an editor that takes over an existing annotation has to be linked to the layer that is live rather than the one that was released.

FR-08.title: Page Layouts
FR-08.note: The layout mode is a property of the virtualizer and not of the page: switching regroups the rows without remounting a page (ViewerPages.regroup), paints nothing again at a fixed zoom (ViewerPages.paint, whose assertions are render calls and canvas backing stores rather than React renders), and — the half that had no assertion, because jsdom sized the viewport at zero and a fit scale resolved against nothing never moves — repaints when the fit target itself moves. That premise is now false: faking the two measurements at the prototype level gives the fit modes a target, and three cases joined the paint file. Continuous to spread at fit-width moves the scale from (viewport - padding) / width to (viewport - padding - gap) / (2 * width) and every page is asked to paint again, every canvas resized. Continuous to single does not move it — the fit target is the same one page across — and no page repaints and no canvas changes size, which is the half of "only when" that an implementation repainting on any layout change would fail. A narrower viewport does move it, including the 640 px padding step, and the pages catch up. The 2026-09-29 Chromium measurement (scale 1.04 to 0.50, every canvas 792×1025 to 386×499) that this row had to cite stands, now with a check that repeats it in jsdom. Four mutations, each restored byte-for-byte: the fit target ignoring the spread (the repaint case red), the fit target assuming two pages always (the no-repaint case red, and the fixed-zoom cases too), and FR-24’s two page wiring mutations, which this file also guards.

FR-09.title: Rotation
FR-09.note: Every overlay layer is asserted to stay registered to the painted page across a rotation — same element, same page index, same layer the editor was handed, one render per layer and no second canvas — and the controller's arithmetic (document-wide, per page, modulo 360, the two adding) is tested through the reducer rather than beside it.

FR-10.title: Outline
FR-10.note: Three clauses, each with an assertion of its own. A click resolves to a page and a position, and the magnification a destination names is taken before the place is measured (outline.test.ts over the real fixture bytes, ViewerController.destination over the wiring that asks the question with the page’s own rotation). The ARIA tree is audited (a11y.audit), which is the clause that was once a styling choice and is now a rule. What had no assertion was the recursion: buildTree is private to usePdfOutline and was called by nothing, while outline.test.ts walked the raw getOutline() array through its own resolveItem helper and the nested trees that reach the DOM in the audit are hand-built OutlineEntry literals. So the shape a reader sees was asserted from a shape nothing parsed. usePdfOutline.tree.test.tsx (8) drives the walk through its only public door and asks the four questions a shallow map gets wrong: three levels come back three levels deep with the leaf’s page resolved; a named destination is asked of getDestination before it is read, and the place it answers is kept rather than dropped; a name the document cannot resolve publishes its entry with no page and its children intact, because the catch is what stops one bad /Dests entry from emptying the sidebar; an object reference is translated at depth, through cachedPageNumber when the engine has one and getPageIndex when it has not, and the 1-based answer is stepped down. Plus /Count read per level, a non-string title that becomes the empty string rather than "undefined", and a document with no outline or a broken one publishing an empty tree instead of an error. Six mutations, each restored byte-for-byte: no recursion (6 cases red), no name resolution, no catch, no /Count, a stringified title, and the cached page number used without the step — each of the last four red on exactly one case.

FR-11.title: Thumbnails
FR-11.note: The card renders at the measured CSS width times the device ratio, tracks the visible range, scrolls the current page into view and gives its buffer back when it leaves — each of those is a failing test in CI now, from observers to the 132 px column arithmetic, and the browser check remains the third look rather than the only one.

FR-12.title: Jump-to-Page
FR-12.note: The row has been `met` while its first verb had no assertion: `page-labels.test.ts` proves a label resolves to a page number and `Toolbar.test.tsx` proves the field clamps, but nothing proved the reader *arrives* on the page they typed. #259 found the hole in webkit (a jump to 1000 landing on 733 for the rest of the session) and #265 fixed it in the virtualizer, where the offset written for a still-measuring document belonged to a table that was about to change. `usePdfVirtualizer.jump.test.tsx` is the guard: the typed page is the page at the top of the viewport after the fit scale lands, after a shrink that clamps the reader, and with a destination inside the page preserved. The acceptance row already cited here, `virtualizes-1000-pages`, is what found the defect; the mechanism it exposed lives under FR-05.

FR-13.title: Text Indexing
FR-13.note: The yield is on the indexing path the shell uses, not only on the utility nothing calls, and it is observed: a rAF ticker counts a fresh frame on every YIELD_PAGES-th page of a supplied-index walk, and a page that never yields stops the counter. Where the read is a worker round trip the round trip is the yield, and the test says which of the two it is watching.

FR-14.title: Match Highlighting
FR-14.note: Native `mark` nodes, the active match’s distinguishing class and `aria-current`, and the non-colour channel that survives forced colours are each asserted (highlight.test.tsx:36-47, a11y.page.test.tsx:164, forced-colors.test.ts:86-93). The third clause — the scroll — is now asserted too, and so is the window around it: src/components/PdfPage.marks.test.tsx installs its own `scrollIntoView` on the prototype (the shell tests stub it away, which is what hid the clause) and holds four things apart: the active element moves and no other, one navigation moves it once however many times the index publishes, a page mounted by scrolling into the range does not move at all, and a request older than the window is not honoured with a jump.

FR-15.title: Search Controls
FR-15.note: Whole-word matching, the counter’s position-within-total and its provisional form were already asserted. The navigation half now is too: the wrap-around is walked in both directions at both ends (and the degenerate one-match and no-match lists stay where they are), and the bar’s buttons are held to the record they hand the matcher — `caseSensitive` and `wholeWord` arriving as `false` when off rather than as absent keys, which is not the same search. Counterfactuals on 2026-10-05: an inverted direction, a clamping end, an option dropped between the call and the plan (both options, separately), a decorative case button and an Enter that re-runs a finished search each failed their test.

FR-16.title: AcroForm Support
FR-16.note: Collecting widgets and reading their types off a real AcroForm fixture is guarded (form.test.ts:46-115), which is the data half. The rendered half is measured rather than read: scripts/browser-matrix.mjs#form-widgets-are-html-controls (added 2026-10-05, #206) loads form-sample.pdf and asserts, per field name, the element the widget became -- input[text] fullName, textarea notes, input[checkbox] subscribe, three input[radio] priority, select[select-one] country, select[select-multiple] skills -- plus that every one of them is focusable (9 controls in 10 boxes, 0 untabbable on the last run). **An acceptance waiver this row carried was wrong and is gone:** it said the control set should be proven in jsdom and that no browser check adds evidence. jsdom does not run pdf.js's AnnotationLayer at all, so a jsdom assertion would have tested a stub; the browser check is the only instrument that can see the elements the clause names. The clause's sixth type was the open half, and #229 closed it on 2026-10-06 by drawing the box in this package instead of asking the engine for one: `SignatureWidgetAnnotationElement` (node_modules/pdfjs-dist/build/pdf.mjs:19170-19173) gives a /Sig widget an element only when `data.hasOwnCanvas`, so five of the fixture's six widgets left the layer with nothing in it and a reader had nothing to aim at. Sampling the painted page canvas inside those five rects reads 0 % ink for four of them; the fifth (`sigAlreadySigned`) reads 4.03 %, because the canvas draws the appearance the file carries for a signed field -- and it gets its box too, since the flags do not predict what the canvas paints (`sigKid` declares an appearance and reads 0 %) and the clause asks for the widget to render as its box rather than for a guess about which fields a reader can already see. `signatureBoxes()` (src/lib/form.ts) now turns each such rect through the page's own viewport into a percentage box and PdfPage mounts them in a pointer-inert `.pjsr-sig-layer`. Measured on the same fixture in all six of CI's engine x profile cells (run 37471520882, dev at 0c79446, 2026-10-06 -- chromium, firefox and webkit at both profiles, 89 ok / 7 skipped / 0 failed, every cell printing the same line). The next run's job went red on this row (CI 37472575777, dev at bfbb973, firefox at the mobile profile) and it was the row's own fault, not the box's: it read page 2's layer before the engine had built its element there, six cells deep in a job that had scrolled and zoomed the document many times over, and said so (`layer classes seen: (none)`). The row now waits for that anchor and prints what was on screen if it never arrives -- proven red by aiming the wait at a selector that cannot exist -- and the run after the fix (CI 37483082866, dev at 781fd88) reads the same six cells green again: 5 boxes drawn and 1 left to the engine, and the box this package draws for the NOROTATE widget agrees with the element the engine positions for it to within 0.002 of the page -- the cross-check that says the viewport math is the engine's math, and it holds through a 90° turn of page 2, where two boxes keep their page share beside the engine's element. The cross-check also corrects the gap text this row deleted: it said **none** of the fixture's /Sig widgets renders anything, which was a detector matching a class containing `sig` rather than a reading of the layer -- the engine does position an element for the one widget whose flag set makes it renderable, and that is the one this rule leaves alone. What stays outside the clause is its own boundary: capturing a mark into a box is FR-29's editing tier, not rendering, and no sig box is a focusable control or takes the pointer -- both asserted.

FR-17.title: Form Data Sync
FR-17.acceptanceWaiver: Two-way binding, plain-object serialisation, reset and dirty tracking are data operations, and they are asserted twice over: on the library against the AcroForm fixture, and on the published hook against a store that mirrors pdf.js’s merge behaviour. A browser would add a rendering claim that FR-16 already carries, and would not be able to say anything about a plain object crossing a hook boundary.
FR-17.note: Two-way write-and-read-back, plain-object serialisation, initial-value reset and dirty comparison are asserted on the library over the AcroForm fixture (form.test.ts:133,168,171,176,179), and now on the surface a host calls: src/headless/usePdfFormValues.test.tsx mounts the hook against a fake store and holds the two binding directions apart — the hook writing {value} under each widget id and bumping version for the layer, and a reader’s keystroke reaching the store without the hook and coming back through refresh(). Radio fan-out across every kid, the read-only refusal, the JSON coercions (a string for a checkbox, a scalar for a list), reset-to-arrival and dirty-by-comparison are each asserted, and eleven counterfactuals each failed the test that names them. One behaviour moved with the guard: version is now bumped only when the writer applied something, because a refused write was claiming a change and re-rendering every mounted annotation layer for nothing.

FR-18.title: Annotations: View
FR-18.note: Verified clause by clause, both halves. Display: — a page hands the engine's own `AnnotationLayer` the document's link, markup and widget annotations and lets it build the DOM, asserted against a stub that records the constructor and the render call separately, because pdf.js reads `annotationEditorUIManager` off one and `renderForms` off the other and a page that passed either to the wrong place looks identical on screen. Two perturbations were run to prove the guard bites: blanking the annotation list, and renaming the layer element; each failed exactly the assertion that clause owns. Withdrawal: fifteen published names leave `.` and `/headless`, the toolbar's `draw` control and the controller's ink state go with them, the core feature contract no longer carries transient strokes, and the core sheet loses the drawing chrome it was never entitled to. The scan reads `src/index.ts` and `src/headless.ts` rather than `dist/` because a name can be missing from an artifact for the wrong reason, and every scan names a control in the same file it is reading. Recorded, not just done: each name is in `api-maturity.json` with the tag it held, the version that drops it and the changelog section that announces it, and `check:maturity` fails if such a name is published again, if its recorded tag is outside the four states, if the version it left in is not a major, or if the section it cites does not name it. Of those four the first met a real artifact rather than a fixture: run against the stale pre-removal `dist/`, the check reported thirty problems, fifteen of them this rule and fifteen `exported and untagged`. The other three fired only in the check's own synthetic set, which grew from nine violations to thirteen to carry them. Two limits belong in the open record rather than in a footnote. One: the changelog warning is the only one there will be, because the PRD plans no published release between `0.1.2` and `1.0.0`, so no minor exists to carry it; `1.0.0` is the first artifact a consumer can install without these names, and the ledger states the tag each held rather than claiming a warning cycle the release plan cannot provide. Two: the shell passed `isPinchingDisabled` to pdf.js's `TouchManager` solely because core drawing wanted every finger, so with core ink gone the predicate was constant-false and it was deleted with its supplier {no behaviour change}. Whether the annotate feature's freehand editor wants the same exemption from a mid-stroke pinch is a question this package did not answer and no jsdom test can: it needs two fingers and a real engine, and it belongs to FR-47's device half.

FR-19.title: High-Fidelity Printing
FR-19.note: The clause’s nouns are a sheet and a hidden application, and both are now measured rather than reasoned about. `print-sheets-hide-the-application` installs its observer at `window.print()` — the one boundary the headless harness cannot cross, since no engine answers the platform dialog and the pipeline tears the container down the moment the call returns — and reads the live DOM from inside it. Five jobs, each in the media its claim belongs to: the selected pages painted (two sheets of a 612×792 pt page at 2.00× = 1,224×1,584 device px, ink 0.36 % and 0.58 %, the scale derived against the fixture’s own MediaBox in Node, not asserted against a constant); the sheet shown and everything else put away in print media (`div.root`, the two script-ish children of body all `display: none`, the container `block`, the second sheet breaking `page`); a typed value reaching the pixels inside its own widget box; a range the reader *typed* ("From–to 2–2") coming back as one sheet, which is the selection a default scope cannot express; and a 1,000-page job refused — no print call, no container, and the error the host receives naming the count that would fit (1,849 MB asked against a 256 MB budget). Chromium and Firefox both ran it green on 2026-10-06 (that host’s four engine×profile cells: 60 ok / 4 skipped / 0 not runnable / 0 failed, the skips being the mobile rows that engine declines), the readings differing the way a rasteriser’s does (0.37 %/0.61 % and 27 → 1,029 dark px in Firefox); webkit 26 joined them on 2026-10-07 on this host, so all three engines have now run the row locally. What the row declines to claim is measured too: dropping `printAnnotationStorage` from the render params leaves the ink delta identical (CF-P1 green in `.spike/counterfactual-fr19.mjs`), because the engine’s print intent falls back to the document’s live `annotationStorage` when it is handed no snapshot (pdfjs-dist/build/pdf.mjs:16494) — the row proves the value arrives, not which storage it arrived from, and the snapshot itself stays pinned where a call record can see it. Three things the row learned about its own harness on the way, all written into it. The first was the fold: choosing "From–to" widens the scope control from 116 to 197 px, and the bar measured whatever state the control happened to be in, so the reader’s own click could move the control — and the two fields it had just revealed — into an overflow panel that nothing had opened. The bar now measures a growing control at its widest state (#243, pinned in `src/components/Toolbar.measure.test.tsx`), which puts the fold decision at load time where a reader can see it, and the number fields are typed and read back rather than merely selected. The second is the media race described above, now retried and reported. The third is that a click cannot be issued in print media at all: Chromium collapses the application’s height and Firefox stops hit-testing the toolbar icon, so once the page is in print the button is pressed through the element rather than clicked. The engine question this row carried as a gap for eleven runs closed on 2026-10-06, and it closed on the rule rather than on a lucky reading: CI 37434962866 (dev at 3206077) and CI 37437044810 (dev at 30b53bf) both drove the whole row green in webkit 26 — 89 ok / 7 skipped / 0 not runnable / 0 failed over six cells, with the same numbers both times (2 sheets at 2.00×, ink 0.36 %/0.57 %, the widget's box 16 → 933 dark px, "Current page" 1 of 2, a typed "From–to 2–2" 1, the 1,000-page refusal) — and `git diff` between those two commits touches only the register and the changelog, so the row that agreed with itself twice is one version of the row. What webkit's readings also say is product, not harness: its own metrics make print's scope group 206 px wide (chromium: 197), so at a 1,246 px bar the page scope *folds* there and is reached through the overflow panel, and Playwright's `selectOption` still times out on a native `<select>` in that engine, so the scope arrives through the `change` event the application listens for — which the row now prints in its own text instead of leaving as an unexplained difference. Four of those eleven runs were mis-reported by this package's own instrument (the print-media emulation race that chromium was also hitting, a closed overflow panel described as an absent control, a read-back whose message re-read the value it had just failed, and a single-frame read of a two-step teardown), and each was fixed by making the row wait for the state its claim is about and print what it saw while waiting. The clause’s marks half arrived the same way on 2026-10-07, in its own row: `print-carries-an-authored-mark` prints a two-page document twice with the scope read back off the control ("all", on every copy, because rows share a page and the print row leaves it on "From–to") and counts one fixed region of page 1’s sheet — 136,699 device px of a 1,224×1,584 page, a fraction of the page rather than a pixel box, since the screen canvas and the sheet are two rasterisations with only the ratio in common. Measured in chromium 153 / firefox 155 / webkit 26 at desktop: that region holds 0 dark px on the first job and 3,338 / 3,365 / 3,179 on the second, after one stroke is drawn with the shipped ink tool and its editor committed, and page 2’s sheet in the same region moves 7,057 → 7,057 / 7,146 → 7,146 / 5,278 → 5,278, which is what makes the delta about the page that was drawn on rather than about a sheet that gained ink somewhere. The pipeline composites nothing — it asks pdf.js for each page at `intent: 'print'` with `AnnotationMode.ENABLE_STORAGE` and hands those canvases over — so an editor-layer mark reaching paper can only mean the engine drew it out of annotation storage, and the row falsifies both halves of that: `AnnotationMode.ENABLE_FORMS` in place of `ENABLE_STORAGE` drops the second reading to 0 px and is reported as "the drawn mark never reached paper", and moving the region onto page 1’s own text fires the premise bar ("the fixture is not blank where this row planned to mark it") at 35,320 px. Two instrument fixes it found on the way, both written into it: the aim has to be resolved after the pen is armed and inside the *scroll element’s* box rather than the window’s, because the playground header sits above the viewer and a first version drew its stroke across a feature checkbox; and the region is a fraction of the page, so the row scrolls the band into view before aiming at it.

FR-20.title: Document Download
FR-20.acceptanceWaiver: Download is a Blob and an object-URL lifecycle; jsdom asserts the branch taken and the filename, and a browser check would observe the same bytes the unit tests already compare.

FR-21.title: Opt-In Feature Registration
FR-21.note: Both gaps this row carried are closed. The three refusals §3.7 names — duplicate id, missing dependency, dependency cycle — now throw `PdfError('CONFIGURATION_ERROR', …)` from `orderFeatures`, which the shell calls before it renders a child and `FeatureRunners` calls again where the runners actually mount, so `before any runner mounts` is a claim with a test behind it rather than a hope: each of the three asserts the recording Runner never ran, and the non-vacuous twin mounts the same list validly to show the recording works. Each removal was counterfactualled in `src/lib/features.ts` — delete the pass, and the guards fail (5, 3 and 6 tests respectively; deleting the ordering fails 7). Two decisions worth keeping. A refusal **throws** rather than routing to `onError`, because a malformed list is a mistake in a component tree and not something that happened to a document, and §3.6 leaves `onError` for the second kind; `useScope()` already threw `CONFIGURATION_ERROR` for a hook used outside a mounted feature, and this row now has that mechanism asserted too. And a list with no `dependsOn` is handed back as *the same array*, because the documented host pattern rebuilds `features` inline on every render and the shell's memos key on it — a fresh array would recompute every page contribution per render, which is a cost no host asked for. The stylesheet half is met as a declaration on the feature value, cross-checked against the export map: 8 built-ins name 8 sheets, `download` names none because its control is the shell's toolbar button, and both directions of drift fail.

FR-22.title: Per-Feature Stylesheets
FR-22.note: Three clauses, each with a gate now. One: a stylesheet per tier is a published entry {nine, classified by `check:packaging`} and each feature declares the ones it ships, which FR-21's contract test walks. Two: the core sheet carries no rule for a feature the application did not request. The rule is computed rather than listed {every `.pjsr-*` class a feature's own source renders and no core source renders must be absent from the built `styles.css`}, which lets a feature extend the core's vocabulary {`pjsr-button`, `pjsr-canvas-wrapper`, the annotation layer element} while refusing it a home in the core sheet. Today 29 classes are feature-only and none is styled by the core; feeding the gate a `.pjsr-annotate-swatch` rule in the core sheet failed it, and the built file was restored by hash. Three: the tree-shaking asymmetry is now asserted where it was only relied on — `sideEffects` must exempt CSS and must not exempt JavaScript, in either direction, because a JS glob in that list keeps every feature in every bundle and a missing CSS entry drops a bare `import 'pdfjs-react-reader/annotate.css'` with no error anywhere. The clause failed before this package for the concrete reason the register named: the core sheet held all the ink chrome (.pjsr-ink rules, the swatch tokens, the inert-annotation rule) while the drawing capability was a feature's job. FR-18 withdrew the surface and the rules went with it, and the withdrawal test asserts the core sheet stays free of it.

FR-23.title: Enforced Size Boundary
FR-23.note: Every path is measured gzipped in CI against a committed baseline, per-tier increments are measured as core + feature − core under two bundlers with the worse number reported, and the core artifact is asserted to contain no feature code. On the owner's ruling of 2026-10-05 the *quantity* checks and the *boundary* checks were separated: growth past the minifier's noise prints GREW and exits 0, and a size number fails only at 200 % of its accepted value (`HARD_STOP` in `scripts/check-size.mjs`), because a budget that blocks feature work is the ceiling §6 forbids. The boundary half is unchanged and still fails at any size — the feature markers that catch a statically imported tier, the requirement that esbuild and Rollup agree, and the FR-22 assertion that `styles.css` carries no feature-only class — so the loosening reached only the byte counts. Both states were measured on throwaway baselines: half of today's `core` yields the `FAIL … 2.00× the accepted … the 200 % stop` line and exit 1, 90 % of it yields `GREW core 31.01 kB gz +3.10 kB` and exit 0. Since #240 the same measurement also *publishes*: `npm run size` writes `docs/src/size-figures.json` - kB per measured path, each feature's increment over core, and the date it was measured - and `Features.tsx`, `Compatibility.tsx` and `Api.tsx` render that file instead of retyping it, so the bytes a reader sees are the bytes the gate measured. `scripts/check-docs.mjs` holds the two together without a bundler: a tier the export map publishes with no figure, a page indexing a key no measurement produced, a `measuredOn` that is not a date, and a size cell typed by hand are each a failure, and `--selftest` writes all of them back in to prove the rule can see them. What it replaced: `annotate` reading 1.86 kB in a docs table against 2.05 kB measured, and a footprint table carrying a `core` from nine releases ago.

FR-24.title: Optional-Content Layers
FR-24.note: Both ends of the clause are measured now: the shared instance by identity in jsdom, and the painted consequence in a browser. The shared-instance clause was a reading of PdfPage.tsx rather than a checked property: setVisibility and usePdfOptionalContent appeared in no test, and both page tests passed optionalContentConfig: null. usePdfOptionalContent.shared.test.tsx (6) pins what the panel does — an injected config means the document is never asked for one (the fetch is the bug the injection exists to avoid), the instance is handed back by identity because that is what a caller passes to render, rows are re-read from the mutable object only when the revision moves because a mutation changes no prop, a SetOCGState action is copied on the way in so a caller reusing its array cannot rewrite what was applied, preserveRB defaults to the engine’s meaning, and a config that throws is reported through onError without asking every page to repaint for a switch that failed. ViewerPages.paint.test.tsx adds the page end: the options each page hands to render carry a promise resolving to the shell’s one instance for all twelve pages, the document is never asked for another, and a layer-less document gets no promise at all rather than an empty one. ViewerController.layers.test.tsx drives the relay the way pdf.js does — through the options the shell hands createPdfLinkService — and reads the consequences back: the instance the controller publishes is the one that moved, the state a panel would now show moved with it, contentVersion grew by one, no second config was fetched, the engine’s array was copied rather than passed through, preserveRB travelled untouched, and a document with no layers drops the action in silence — no repaint and no error, which is what makes the guard in front of the relay load-bearing rather than defensive. Eight mutations, each restored byte-for-byte: no repaint after the action, the action’s array passed through, preserveRB decided for the document, the relay run with no config, a panel that fetches its own config, a panel that hands back a copy, a panel that passes the array through, and a failed switch that still repaints. Every one of them red, one case each. What no jsdom could say is now said by pixels: `layers-switch-paints-a-page` reads horizontal bands of the live canvas on `attachments-ocg-sample.pdf`, each band a distance from the top of the page in the document's own units converted against `basePageDims()`, where the fixture puts exactly one line of text in each group and nothing else at that height. In chromium 153 / firefox 155 / webkit 26, desktop 1280×900: the three groups are listed with the states `/OCProperties` declares them in (Heading on, Body on, Stamp off), the Stamp band is 0 dark px while its group is off with the three neighbouring bands painted (2,558 / 1,485 / 1,974 in chromium), 5,245 px after one switch on and back to 0 after one switch off, and page 2's grouped line follows the *same panel* to 0 px and back to 1,277 px while its ungrouped neighbour never moves — that last leg is the clause's "every page", and a config fetched per render would leave page 2 on the document's defaults (5,265 and 1,299 in firefox, 5,084 and 1,176 in webkit). Three counterfactuals, each red for the reason its own message names and restored byte-for-byte: `optionalContentConfig={null}` on the page, so every render asks for its own instance, fails at "the checkbox moved and the page did not"; dropping the hook's `onChanged?.()`, so no revision ever moves, fails a leg earlier at "a list that cannot see the state it just wrote"; and a panel that reports every group visible fails the listing premise before any pixel is read. Two instrument defects the row found in itself: Playwright's `check()` reads a controlled checkbox on the tick after the click, before React's commit has put the new state on the element, so a switch is now clicked and then *waited for*; and the premise was one unpolled canvas read, which webkit's cell reported as a page that painted nothing — the bands are waited for now, and a page that never paints is named as the missing premise rather than as a layer defect. Reaching the Layers tab was itself a finding, and this row is what surfaced it: `.pjsr-sidebar-tabs` was a no-wrap flex row inside a 248 px panel, so with three tabs the third ran past the tablist and the close control — a later sibling in DOM order — painted over it, and `elementFromPoint` at its centre answered `button.pjsr-sidebar-close` in chromium (198,206) and webkit (198,181); firefox's metrics let the pointer land. The first version of the row fell back to the tablist's own ArrowRight keys and printed which path it took, which is a keyboard reader's route hiding a mouse user's defect. So #254 was filed and the same pass fixed it: the tablist now wraps, the row *requires* a pointer click, and removing `flex-wrap` makes it fail naming #254 and the covering element. With the rule in place all three engines report "took a pointer click", and a four-tab mount (Thumbnails, Outline, Layers, Attachments) reads a 90 px header in two rows with every tab reaching.

FR-25.title: Embedded Files
FR-25.acceptanceWaiver: The list and the saved bytes are proven against the real engine on playground/fixtures/attachments-ocg-sample.pdf in Node, and the save is asserted down to the anchor click and the Blob it hands the browser; the matrix mounts no attachments UI, so a browser check would re-run the engine call the fixture test already makes.

Listing still reads zero contents, which is the prefetch clause made observable.

FR-26.title: Replaceable Find Strategy
FR-26.note: The seam was real and unexercised: find ?? builtInSearch at ViewerController.tsx:450, typed as PdfFindController on PdfViewer’s props, with the only PdfFindController in the suite being ViewerController.search.test.tsx’s own mock return value for usePdfSearch and the host-shaped stub in SearchBox.counter.test.tsx going straight into SearchBox. So nothing proved the clause — that an alternative strategy is passed in rather than built around, and that a host keeping the built-in bar, marks and counts does not have to fork the shell. ViewerController.find.test.tsx (5) supplies a host controller to the shell and asserts the five things that makes true: the object the shell publishes is the host’s, by identity (a merged wrapper would be a second opinion on every field, and the bar reads what the shell publishes); the matches are grouped per page from the host’s results and the active local index comes from the host’s activeIndex; a query asked of the shell reaches the host’s search and no page’s text is read, which is the difference between the host’s strategy running and both running with the built-in’s answer on screen; without a host controller the same question does open the pages, so the previous claim is not a search that silently did nothing; and a host publishing new results re-marks the pages on the next render without the shell being asked again. Three mutations, each restored byte-for-byte: the seam ignored (all five cases red), the host merged into a shell-built wrapper (the identity case red), and the marks grouped from the built-in’s results even while a host drove the find (two cases red).

FR-27.title: Search Depth
FR-27.note: AND-per-page over escaped literals, raw regex where the reader wrote it, per-page counts, and cancellation of a superseded or aborted walk were all met before this row was revisited; the ceiling was the one clause with no code. It is now `DEFAULT_MAX_PATTERN_UNITS`, checked before `new RegExp` and overridable per query with `maxPatternUnits`, with the two refusals distinguishable as `patternKind: too-long | invalid` beside the sentence in `patternError`. Three things the tests hold that are easy to get wrong: a pattern that is both over the limit and malformed reports `too-long`, which is the proof the length gate ran first; a refused pattern reads `status: error` with `complete: true` and an empty result set, so only the status and the kind separate it from a genuine no-match; and a long *literal* query is never bounded, because its cost is in the text scanned, not in what was typed. The bound is a trade, not a virtue — the row excludes worker isolation and a per-page deadline from the `1.0.0` contract, so nothing else stands between a reader’s `(a+)+$` and a frozen tab.

FR-28.title: Composed Shell, Labels, Events, Locales & Shell Affordances
FR-28.note: The composed-shell, labels, events and locales clauses have held since 0.5 and 0.2; what pulled this row back was the sentence about the shell’s own affordances, which named five props that no test ever passed as false. ViewerController.affordances.test.tsx (9) refuses them one at a time against the composed shell — the real Toolbar inside ViewerLayout, because a bar the test never rendered cannot show whether a control is missing from it — and reads the refusal back off the chrome: a refused wheel leaves the scale alone and is not preventDefaulted, so the host page keeps the scroll, while the same gesture taken unconditionally zooms and reports defaultPrevented true; a refused pinch changes nothing and does not claim the touchmove; a refused keyboard leaves PageDown and ArrowDown unclaimed, which is the claim the clause makes about who owns the key (with no document mounted the page cannot move, so the enabled leg is asserted as the prevented counterpart rather than as a page change); a refused fullscreen hides the control — counted on the bar and not on the measuring copy in .pjsr-toolbar-sizer, which is why a query that names a control without naming its bar resolves twice — reports fsAvailable false, and never reaches the element’s requestFullscreen; and a refused drop leaves the page’s own dragover alone and never shows the drop highlight, while an enabled one claims the event, puts pjsr-viewer--dragover on the root and hands the file to onDropFile. That last pair is where the read found a defect rather than a missing test: enableFullscreen only ever hid the button, while the published imperative handle’s toggleFullscreen went straight to the element, so a host that refused the affordance could still be fullscreened by its own code. toggleFullscreen now returns when the prop says the affordance is off, which is the change the row’s word for this is “refused”. Six mutations, each restored byte-for-byte: every one of the five guards removed, plus the bar showing the control anyway — each red on the case that names it, and none of them red anywhere in the gesture file, because the enabled half was never the untested part. Measured 2026-10-06 (#175, ViewerLayout.ready.test.tsx): the shell now mounts under jsdom against a document that has finished loading, so the two legs that needed a page on screen are asserted instead of described -- PageDown moves the reader 1 -> 2, the bar's own field follows, `onPageChange` sees the number, and a refused keyboard leaves the page, the scroll position and the event all untouched, which is the sentence this row used to have to satisfy with `defaultPrevented` alone. The harness (`src/components/ready-shell-harness.tsx`, shared with FR-45's ready audit since #247, with the page proxy kept apart from it in `ready-fake-document.ts` for the mock-cycle reason that file names) answers four things jsdom does not give: a `ResizeObserver` that reports an entry (`ThumbnailList.tsx:30` reads `entries[0].contentRect.width`, so calling back with nothing throws outside the test's own frames and surfaces as an unhandled error rather than a failure -- that is how the first version of this file told the truth and still failed the suite), an `IntersectionObserver` for the thumbnail rows, a sized viewport, and the `scrollTo`/`scrollTop` pair the virtualizer's loop runs on. **Two claims this row carried are withdrawn by that run.** The first, in README and CODE_REFERENCE §20, was that mounting a ready document *hangs* jsdom (measured twice to a 60 s and a 120 s kill): re-measured, nothing hangs -- the shell mounts in ~330 ms, and real bytes fail fast instead, on `Uint8Array.prototype.toHex` and `Map.prototype.getOrInsertComputed`, two methods pdf.js 6.3.289 calls that Node v24.21.0 does not have. So what remains is an engine ceiling rather than a harness one, the paint stays the browser matrix's, and the document here is a page proxy of the kind the nine `PdfPage.*` files already build. The second: a counterfactual that made the observer stop reporting intersection **passed**, which showed the thumbnail count measures the list mounting rather than anything painting, so the stub was cut back to an idle one and the claim narrowed to what it reads. Five counterfactuals fail their own case: ignoring the keyboard refusal, unwiring `onPageChange`, removing the bar's page-mirroring effect, moving `scrollToPage` one row early, and turning the harness's `scrollTo` into a no-op -- the last naming the fake as what lets the page move, so the geometry assertions are the shell's and the scroll pair is the harness's.

FR-29.title: Annotation Authoring
FR-29.note: The row read met on a browser pass made during 0.6 and no guard, and its first gap — `annotateFeature` is never mounted by a test — had itself gone stale: annotate.armed.test.tsx mounts the feature and guards the tool-to-mode arithmetic. What was missing was the rest of the sentence. annotate.lifecycle.test.tsx now owns it in jsdom: the manager is constructed with the document whose `annotationStorage` an incremental save commits, is built once per document and rebuilt-and-disposed on a swap, survives page churn untouched while the page's own layer is rebuilt against the same instance, takes its alert region down with it, and cannot arm any engine mode outside the three tools offered. The two clauses jsdom cannot reach — a real mark reaching real bytes, and a mark surviving a real page leaving the window — are measured in Chromium by the matrix row, which draws one stroke, jumps to page 14, proves page 1's editor element left the document and came back, then saves through the viewer's own Download control and re-opens the bytes with the engine to count the `/Ink` annotation against a fixture that carries none. Measured: four jsdom counterfactuals (2, 1, 2 and 8 failures) and two browser ones — a page that disposes the document-wide manager breaks the row and 3 cells, and a download that decides there are no edits fails it naming the 24,378-byte file as carrying 0 ink annotations. One more came out of the new rows' own state churn (#257): the manager was constructed with the viewer root as its container, and pdf.js gates its Enter and Space editor bindings on `container.contains(target)` before reading `currentLayer.canCreateNewEmptyEditor()` with no guard — so a key typed in the toolbar or the sidebar could reach a handler written for a key pressed *on a page*, and throw uncaught whenever no page layer was current (webkit · desktop threw it twice on 2026-10-07, in a document swap, and the cell-level `no-uncaught-errors` check could not say which row did it). The container is the pages' scroller now, with the root only as the fallback a host writing its own layout needs, and `src/features/annotate.container.test.tsx` (3) asserts the containment shape rather than the crash, because the crash is timing-sensitive and the wiring is not.

FR-30.title: Page Authoring
FR-30.acceptanceWaiver: Reorder, delete, rotate, extract and split are asserted by writing real files and re-opening them in jsdom, and so is both-level undo: the assertion reads the page tree out of the bytes handed to the shell. A browser pass would produce the same evidence about the same bytes at higher cost, and would add nothing the tier’s clause claims.
FR-30.note: Reorder, delete, rotate, extract and split are guarded against written bytes and re-opened in jsdom (page-plan.test.ts, pdf-write.test.ts:118-162, edit.extract.test.tsx:156, which asserts two files with the right page kids). Both undo levels are now executed by a test (src/edit.undo.test.tsx): the snapshot an apply started from comes back byte for byte, the level spends itself, what an apply holds is the last apply’s snapshot and not the first, and the view rotations return as view state. The batching is tallied on the writer’s own entry point — three edits cost no read and no parse, the apply that follows costs one of each. Nine counterfactuals were run against these guards on 2026-10-05 and each failed the test that names it.

FR-31.title: True Flattening
FR-31.acceptanceWaiver: Flattening is asserted on written files by re-reading them, including the missing-appearance case that made unsigned forms throw; there is nothing a browser check would see that the bytes do not already show.
FR-31.note: Amended 2026-10-04: the clause now names what the writer does — supported widgets and supported signature appearances, markup annotations carried through untouched — because `PDFForm.flatten()` walks `getFields()` and their widgets and never sees a non-widget annotation (@cantoo/pdf-lib/cjs/api/form/PDFForm.js:635-657). No clause of the restated requirement changed its evidence.

FR-32.title: Visual Signing
FR-32.acceptanceWaiver: A written mark painting in both file-borne and in-session documents was browser-verified during the signing spike and recorded in the changelog; the matrix carries no signing check yet, which is tracked rather than claimed here. What the clause states is about bytes and about a sentence on screen while a parse runs, and both are asserted against real files in jsdom.
FR-32.note: The mark reaching an appearance stream, the `/V` count proving no signature value is written, the `ALREADY_SIGNED` refusal on both the writer and the built-in pad, and the deferred one-parse scan are each asserted. The plural is now asserted too: `signature-sample.pdf` grew a fifth field whose `/Kids` name two widgets on two pages at two sizes (2026-10-05), so one mark resolved into four different page numbers is what `pdf-write.test.ts` reads back, and the panel says `· 2` out loud because a reader who signed the first box would otherwise check the second and conclude it failed. `reported while it runs` is asserted by holding the scan’s bytes behind a deferred and reading the status line while it is still unpaid.

FR-33.title: XFA Display, Save Refused
FR-33.acceptanceWaiver: The save refusal is a branch and a resolved value, both asserted against a stubbed engine whose `saveDocument()` rejection was measured on all three /XFA container shapes in 0.7; the half of that clause a browser could add is a download dialog this harness cannot read.
FR-33.note: Four clauses, each with an assertion of its own now. The save refusal is a resolved value rather than an error: `download()` answers `{ fileName, committed, refused }`, the hook publishes `refused`, `onRefused` is there for a caller that does not await, and the built-in control puts the reason in its accessible name — which is in the catalog, so it is in German, Spanish and French too. The viewport clause has held since `PdfPage.xfa.test.tsx`: `XfaLayer.render` *appends*, so a zoom that re-rendered doubled the page and cost the reader their focused field; the page keeps its div and calls `update`. A driven browser said the same through two rotations. The guard stays as defence for a call site that does not exist yet, and the row says so rather than counting it as a tested branch. The browser half is the matrix's `sidebar-thumbs-outline` row, which now loads the pure-XFA fixture and reads what jsdom cannot: the tree the engine laid out, its measured box, its `inert` state and its tab order, and the same card after the document has been turned twice.

FR-34.title: Network Contract
FR-34.acceptanceWaiver: Bearer, cookie and signed-URL loading was proven by hand against scripts/auth-server.mjs, a dev-only server; the browser matrix refuses the network by design, so its evidence would be a CDN assertion, not an auth one.

FR-35.title: Bounded Retries
FR-35.acceptanceWaiver: Every clause is observable in the node harness and asserted there: the status set the classifier retries and refuses, the default intervals, the per-attempt reports including the final one, and — under fake timers — that an abort during a five-second wait clears the timer outright. The browser matrix drives a successful load and a refused one; it injects no transient failure, so a browser row here would describe a check that does not exist.
FR-35.note: Three attempts, one second first, thirty-second ceiling, full jitter, 408/425/429 and 5xx plus no-response retried and 401/403/404/corrupt/encrypted never retried — all of it was already true and already tested. What was not true is recorded here because the shape of the failure is the lesson: the two delay defaults sat at 250 ms and 5 s for a whole release with the row saying 1 s and 30 s, because every existing test passed its own policy in and so could not observe the shipped numbers. The guard added with this row calls `backoffDelay` with `{ jitter: false }` and nothing else, which is the only form of the call that reads the defaults. Two decisions worth having written down: a host that passes `retry: false` gets no attempt report at all (one attempt is not a retry story, and it reaches the host as an `AUTH_ERROR`-class failure instead), and the wait wakes on the load effect’s own `AbortController`, which every stop path aborts — unmount, superseded source and host signal — rather than on the host signal alone, because an unmount has to stop the timer too.

FR-36.title: Cancellation Tokens
FR-36.acceptanceWaiver: Cancellation is a lifecycle fact, not a painted one: what the clause asks is observable as engine calls that did not happen, buffers that were released and bytes that never arrive — all of which jsdom counts exactly, and a browser cannot distinguish from a slow frame. The React 18 and 19 halves are the same suite run twice, which is what the react-18 CI job does; the browser matrix runs the viewer on three engines but has no abort to issue.
FR-36.note: The clause is a list of operations — load, page proxy, render, extraction, indexing, thumbnail, print render, download, every writer pass — and it reads as one promise, which is how a single sentence can hold nine operations and still leave three of them unasserted. Each entry now has a test that aborts it and counts what did not happen. Writing the assertions for the last three found three half-gaps in the code, and the code moved rather than the sentence: `usePdfPrint` never checked a token that had already fired before the job began, and read `signal` from the render that built the callback rather than the one the host holds when it calls; the attachment walk published whatever it had reached *as a complete list* when an abort landed mid-walk, and read the catalog at all for a token born aborted; and a card mounted into an already-cancelled sidebar fetched its page anyway. All three were fixed before their cases were kept, and seven mutations — each one line of that guard — now fail exactly the case that names them. The clause's own comparison is asserted too: an aborted card ends in the same state as a scrolled-out one, says nothing through `onError`, and cancels the running render rather than releasing only the buffer. Two things stay honestly narrower than the sentence sounds: a writer loop stops *before its next page* and cannot un-make a page already rearranged inside the peer (asserted as such, with the output always suppressed), and an in-flight `getPage` is not interruptible, so the walk stops at the next check it owns.

FR-37.title: Published State Models
FR-37.note: The gap this row carried was that `destroyed` has no observable path, and the reading of §3.5 settled it rather than a test: the member is written by exactly two paths — an unmount, whose state update React drops because the component reading it is gone, and a supersede, which co-commits `destroyed` and the next `loading` into one commit — so it is terminal and unobservable *by definition*, not by omission. §3.5 now says that in its own words and FR-37 names it the one exception to “both unions are produced”, because the alternative was to manufacture a render or a reporter whose only customer would be the assertion. `src/headless/usePdfDocument.status.test.tsx` holds the boundary with a measurement rather than a claim: it records the sequence a host can read and asserts the word is not in it, and the counterfactual that opened the row — every teardown claiming `cancelled` fails nothing, while every teardown claiming `destroyed` fails the host-cancel case — is why the sentence is about the surface and not about coverage. Everything else in the clause was already held: the unions are published types, the ready-with-null-handle invariant is built into `PdfDocumentLoad` rather than policed, `cancelled` never passes through `error`, the password path parks with its reason, the page retry §3.5 promises is published and reaches the model, and all seven page states are written by a path a test drives.
FR-37.acceptanceWaiver: Both unions are produced by components under test rather than declared and unreachable: the document path is driven through a host `AbortSignal` and a password prompt in jsdom, and the page path through fake render tasks whose settle and failure the test controls. What a browser would add — real scroll-out timing — is covered as behaviour by FR-04’s checks, not as a state the model can only show on a device.

FR-38.title: Source Utilities
FR-38.acceptanceWaiver: base64ToBytes and classifySource are pure functions over strings; the browser cannot add evidence about a heuristic that never touches the DOM, and both barrels export them so the packaging check covers reachability.

FR-39.title: Incremental, Viewport-Prioritised Indexing

What remains a design decision rather than a defect: `RENDER_CANCELLED` is produced only by classification, because every call site that catches the engine’s cancellation returns before the wrapper — FR-36’s rule that a cancellation is not an ordinary failure, and a page whose paint was stopped reports `cancelled` through `onStatusChange` instead. A Chromium probe measured that `RenderTask.cancel()` is the only way a render is cancelled at all (a second proxy rendering the same page, `cleanup()` on either proxy, and a second render over the same canvas all left the first task fulfilled), so the code is a diagnosis for a case the package prevents, and it is written that way rather than as a promise a host should handle.

FR-55.title: Worker & Source Security Contract
FR-55.note: Worker configuration, the one-per-realm rule and the source policy were already asserted at the library boundary and in a browser (nothing reached a CDN). Both halves that were missing are now pinned. `enableScripting: false` is read off the annotation layer’s *render* params, not its constructor, and deleting it left the suite green until today; the test checks every render call the page makes, because a second path that forgets the flag is the same hole as the first having it removed. And a host’s `allowedSources` is followed from the prop to the engine decision — which is where an option gets dropped: an allowed origin reaches `getDocument` with its href intact, a refused one surfaces `SOURCE_NOT_ALLOWED` naming the origin (never the query string, where a signed URL keeps its credential) with `getDocument` never called. One stale detail in the gap text was corrected on the way: the literal exists at exactly one site, not two. Two counterfactuals, each failing the test that names it.

FR-56.title: Feature Lifecycle Contract
FR-56.note: All eight §3.7 obligations now have code and an assertion: stable id, declared dependencies, registration lifecycle (`Runner` mounts, the store retires, `cleanup` releases), the capabilities a feature is handed (`PdfViewerShell`), declared stylesheet entries, duplicate-registration behaviour, missing/cyclic-dependency behaviour, and ordering rules where ordering is observable. Three things are recorded here because they are the parts that could have been faked. **No built-in declares `dependsOn` or `cleanup`, and none should.** The nine tiers are genuinely independent — `download` asks `forms` and `annotate` whether the document has edits and works when neither answers, which is a peer read through `usePdfFeaturePeer`, not a dependency; declaring one there would refuse a composition that is correct today. The dependency machinery is therefore proven with written features, and the two observable consequences of it are pinned where they can be seen: initialisation order, and which feature wins a page contribution (the dependent) versus which claims a chord (the dependency) — both asserted against what the *written* order would have answered, so the sort is doing the work rather than the fixture. **`cleanup` runs before the Runner's own effect teardown**, because React destroys a deleted subtree's passive effects parent-first; that was measured rather than assumed, it is asserted so the documentation cannot rot quietly, and it is why the field is for resources the component never held. **The import boundary is asserted in source, not only in the bundle.** `scripts/check-size.mjs` already refuses a feature marker in the core bundle under two bundlers; `src/lib/feature-boundary.test.ts` names the offending import, and it scans the AST rather than the text because this project's own doc comments quote specifiers. Its positive control proves the scanner is not blind: the allowed edges (`src/edit.tsx` → `./features/ids`, `annotate` → the contract) are found, the type-only cross-tier import is classified as erased, and adding a real violation to any tier fails it — verified with two counterfactual imports, both restored.

FR-57.title: Runtime Resource Budget Contract
FR-57.note: The four §6.1 ceilings now combine as a minimum and the platform-safe one is probed rather than labelled. Measured by `npm run probe:canvas` on Chromium (pdfjs-dist 6.3.289, 2026-10-03): a 1280x800 @1x page answers 3,072,000 px, which is its viewport working set and below the desktop default, so the probe confirmed the ceiling in force instead of raising it; an iPad user agent on a 390x844 @3x screen lowers the start to 5,242,880 and the answer follows it; a search forced to 1,048,576 never answers above it. The shell's own search costs ~80 ms spread over six frames with one surface per frame and its first surface ~3 ms after the page's first paint, which is what `canvas.probe.test.ts` and the harness both hold. A host budget constrains and `renderBudget.applied` names which ceiling won; a page that cannot be represented at MIN_RENDER_SCALE 0.25 is refused with RESOURCE_LIMIT rather than left blank. §6.1's 'Viewport working-set factor | 200 %, host-configurable' row is the second host input and had no host path until #222 gave it one, so it is constrained the same way: `capAreaFactor` is accepted below the package's 200 and clamped at it above — lifting the working set is switching the term off rather than tuning it, and a `NaN` would erase it silently because `Math.min` answers `NaN` — `CanvasBudget.capAreaFactor` reports the number actually used, and the same clamp bounds the probe's search limit, not only the budget the pages paint under.

FR-58.title: Release Evidence & Consumer Verification
gaps: the chain now exists and is guarded, and it has still never run. `npm run check:upgrade` installs the registry’s current release into a throwaway consumer, applies the packed candidate over it the way a host would, and then reads back the lockfile, the peer resolutions and every published name a 0.1.2 host could reach — a name that vanishes is a failure unless `api-maturity.json`’s `removed` ledger already announced it, which is the shape §5.5 promises and the shape FR-18’s fifteen withdrawn ink names satisfy. `scripts/rc-record.mjs` writes the candidate record, refusing a leg that is absent, a leg no job produces, a `success` with no run id or artifact digest behind it, and any attempt to write the word `certified` (§9 is signed by a person). `.github/workflows/release-candidate.yml` runs the seven legs on Node 22.13.0 and 24 against the artifact — `verify`, FR-41’s tarball proof, §5.6’s examples, the upgrade, the browser matrix at `dist/`, the axe audit, the two bench passes — and uploads what it recorded. What is not yet evidence is the run itself: no `release/last-candidate*.json` is committed, because the first candidate has to be dispatched or tagged, and `ci.yml` only grew `tags: [‘v*’]` so a tag also runs the React and engine axes this job does not. The guard proves the writers refuse to lie, not that the chain passes.

the real-device pass and the three screen-reader pairings have no environment, no schedule and no artifact; §9 says that is the reason 1.0.0 has not shipped rather than a thing to defer, and `#141` and #273 are where they are tracked

the upgrade’s *own* boundary, stated rather than glossed: `check:upgrade` migrates the `pdfjs-react-reader` entry and asserts the peers the candidate declares are still satisfied — it does not migrate a consumer’s application code, and it cannot, because a public API change is §5.5’s major-version rule and not a test. §9’s phrase "including lockfile/dependency migration and public API checks" is therefore met for the dependency half and the published-surface half, and the third thing a reader might want from it — "my app still behaves" — is what the browser matrix and the examples check cover, on the artifact, in the same job.
FR-58.note: Moved from `absent` to `partial` by #272 on 2026-10-09: the two clauses that were code-free — "validate upgrade from the previous public release" and "recorded with its environment, operator and date" — now have a script each, a job that runs them, and a guard that names `FR-58` and refuses the record shapes that would make a green meaningless. Measured locally on the day it was written: 0.1.2 → 0.11.0, lockfile migrated, 2 published entries before and 15 after, 15 root names and 7 headless names gone with the ledger announcing every one of them, and 79/63 names gained; `PJSR_TARGET=dist` reports `library copy under test: dist (41 artifact module(s), 0 source module(s))` and the matrix’s rows pass against the build. Two falsifications ran against the new guards: removing `./headless` from the export map makes the upgrade check fail with "a published entry point cannot disappear in a minor" (manifest restored by checksum), and deleting an `if: always()` from a leg step reddens the wiring case. What remains is a run: the chain has never executed, so the row cannot be `implemented` until a candidate has produced a record.
